summary: Defines how the Extensible Provisioning Protocol handles contacts, meaning individuals or organizations with social information identifiers, in a shared registry. It specifies command syntax and semantics for contact objects. It obsoletes an earlier version and is an Internet Standard.

eli5.summary: This is the EPP rulebook chapter about people and companies, saying how a registry stores who is responsible for a name, and how those details are added or changed.

questions: what is an epp contact object
how are phone numbers written in epp
how does epp contact disclosure work
subtitle: How a domain registry stores the people and organizations behind domain names, over EPP.

tldr.problem: A registry needs a standard way to record who is responsible for a name, including postal address, phone, email and what may be shown to others, in a form many registrars can use.
tldr.mechanism: The mapping defines a contact object with an identifier, one or two postal-info blocks, phone, fax, email, a password-style authorization value and optional disclosure flags, and says how EPP check, info, create, delete, transfer and update apply to it.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 4933. The authorization information must be protected, since leaking it can allow unauthorized transfers and information release.

today: RFC 5733 is an Internet Standard published in August 2009. It obsoletes RFC 4933, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What a Contact Object Is
sections.content:
RFC 5733 describes a personal and organizational identifier mapping for version 1.0 of the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP). It is specified in XML and XML Schema and depends on the base protocol in RFC 5730.

A contact object is a record in a shared repository for a person or organization. It is identified by a server-unique identifier that follows the clIDType syntax from RFC 5730, and its attributes can be viewed and modified by the sponsoring client or the server.
sections.eli5: A contact is a card in the registry's card box with someone's name, address and phone. Every card gets its own unique label.

sections.title: Contact Attributes
sections.content:
Names and addresses can be given in UTF-8 or in a subset that fits 7-bit ASCII. An address has optional street, city, optional state or province, an optional postal code and a required country identifier, which is a two-character code from ISO 3166-1.

Telephone numbers are strings that MUST begin with a plus sign, then a country code from ITU E.164, then a dot, then the digits, with an optional x attribute for an extension. Email syntax follows RFC 5322, and the mapping sets no length limits for it. Dates and times MUST be UTC in the extended form with upper case T and Z.

Each postal-info block has a type: int (internationalized) content MUST fit 7-bit US-ASCII, while loc (localized) content MAY be unrestricted UTF-8. One or two blocks may be given, so the same address can be stored in both forms.
sections.eli5: A card can hold the address twice, once in plain letters anyone can read and once in the home alphabet. Phone numbers follow a fixed style that starts with a plus sign.

sections.title: Status Values
sections.content:
As with hosts, a contact MUST always have at least one status value, and the client, server and server-managed prefixes decide who may change each one. Besides the delete and update prohibitions, contacts also have clientTransferProhibited and serverTransferProhibited, which mean transfer requests MUST be rejected.

The linked status says the contact is attached to another object, such as a domain, and ok may be combined only with linked. The four pending values mark an action the server has accepted but not yet completed, and they MUST NOT be combined with each other. pendingTransfer cannot be combined with the transfer prohibitions.
sections.eli5: Stickers on the card say things like Locked or Waiting. This chapter adds a Do Not Move sticker, because cards can be moved between companies.

sections.title: The Commands
sections.content:
<check> asks whether contact identifiers can be provisioned. <info> returns the identifier, a repository object identifier, statuses, postal info, voice, fax, email, client and date fields, and the authorization info, but the authorization info MUST NOT be included if the querying client is not the current sponsor.

<create> needs an identifier, at least one postal-info block, an email and authorization information. The schema allows new authorization mechanisms, but this mapping includes a password-based one.

<update> can add or remove statuses and change postal info, phone, fax, email, authorization info and disclosure settings. At least one of add, rem or chg MUST be given unless the command is extended.

<delete> SHOULD NOT remove a contact that is still associated with other objects, and the server SHOULD send error 2305 when a delete fails for that reason. There is no <renew> mapping.
sections.eli5: You can check if a label is free, read a card, write a new one, fix one or throw one away. Throwing away a card that is still being used is not a good idea.

sections.title: Transfer and Offline Review
sections.content:
Unlike hosts, contacts have their own <transfer> command. The request carries the contact identifier and its authorization information, and an op attribute whose operations are defined in RFC 5730. A query form reports the state of the most recent request: its status, the requesting client, the date requested, the client that should act on a pending request, and the response deadline or completion date.

As with other EPP objects, a server MAY defer a transform command for human or third-party review. It returns code 1001, sets a matching pending status, and later sends a service message with a panData element whose paResult attribute says whether the request was approved or denied. Unauthorized transforms MUST be rejected with code 2201.
sections.eli5: A card can be handed from one company to another if you know the secret password. If someone has to check first, you get a note telling you to wait, and a second note with the answer.

sections.title: Disclosure Preferences
sections.content:
The EPP core protocol requires a server operator to announce data-collection policies. This mapping lets a client mark contact data that needs exceptional handling by adding an optional <contact:disclose> element when creating or updating a contact.

Its flag attribute is a boolean: 1 or true means the named elements may be disclosed as an exception to the policy, and 0 or false means they may not. It MUST contain at least one child, which can be name, org or addr (in int or loc form), voice, fax or email. A server MUST reject a request that conflicts with its announced policy with error 2308.
sections.eli5: You can tell the registry which parts of your card strangers may see and which parts stay hidden, as long as that fits the registry's own rules.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Authorization information is REQUIRED to create a contact and is used in some query and transfer operations. Failure to protect it from inadvertent disclosure can result in unauthorized transfer operations and unauthorized information release. Both client and server MUST ensure it is stored and exchanged with high-grade encryption mechanisms.

Otherwise the mapping adds no security services beyond those in RFC 5730 or the protocol layers beneath EPP.
sections.eli5: The secret password on a card is what proves you own it, so it has to be kept in a locked box. If someone learns it, they could move your card away.
